{{Short description|Open problem in computer science}}
{{unsolved|computer science|If the expansion of a real <math>x</math> in some base <math>b \geq 2</math> is real-time computable, must <math>x</math> be rational or transcendental?}}

In [[theoretical computer science]] and [[mathematics]], the '''Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture''' is an open problem named after [[Juris Hartmanis]] and [[Richard E. Stearns]], who posed it in a 1965 paper that founded the field of [[computational complexity theory]]{{r|original}} (earning them the 1993 [[ACM Turing Award]]).

An [[infinite word]] is said to be ''real-time computable'' when there exists a [[multitape Turing machine]] which (run without input) writes the successive letters of the word on its output tape, taking a bounded amount of time between two successive letters. Equivalently, there exists a multitape Turing machine which given a natural number <math>n</math> in unary outputs the first <math>n</math> letters of the word in time <math>O(n)</math>.{{r|fmr|lipton-blog}} The Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture states that if <math>x</math> is a real number whose expansion in some base <math>b \geq 2</math> (e.g., the [[decimal expansion]] for <math>b = 10</math>) is real-time computable, then <math>x</math> is [[rational number|rational]] or [[transcendental number|transcendental]].{{r|acg|lipton-blog}}

The conjecture has the deep implication that there is no [[integer multiplication algorithm]] in <math>O(n)</math> (while an <math>O(n \log(n))</math> algorithm is known).{{r|lipton-blog}}

A partial result was proved by Boris Adamczewski and Yann Bugeaud{{r|adamczewski-bugeaud}} (a previous claimed proof by John H. Loxton and [[Alfred van der Poorten]]{{r|loxton-poorten}} turned out to contain a gap): <math>x</math> is rational or transcendental if the expansion of <math>x</math> in some base <math>b \geq 2</math> is an [[automatic sequence]]. This was subsequently generalized by Boris Adamczewski, Julien Cassaigne and Marion Le Gonidec{{r|acg}} to sequences generated by [[deterministic pushdown automata]].
